A.2 Thresholds and Tension
Θexist Existence thresholds: minimal conditions for Ω(K) 6= ;.
Θstab Stability thresholds: conditions for bounded dynamics.
Θcrit Critical thresholds: surfaces of qualitative change or phase transition.
Θdim Dimensional thresholds: conditions for emergence of new axes.
Θtime Temporal-stability threshold used in K-level time-emergence clauses. A cycle contributes to scalar level-time only when
its persistence or closure score satisfies the local Π(Cj) > Θtime obligation.
Θdeath Death thresholds: limits beyond which no admissible states remain.
Θexpr Expressive thresholds: minimal expressive capacity of axes required to represent relevant differences.
Θembed Embedding thresholds: constraints imposed by embedding spaces Mx.
T (K, t) Structural tension functional, depending on potentials, axes and gradients.
A.3 Operators
The time-indexed operators below describe internal dynamics for levels K1 and above on time slices of a fixed continuum K.
The K0-local glyphs and cross-level birth operators listed later are separate namespaced entries, not members of that internal-
dynamics family. Level K0 is non-dynamical and carries no internal time parameter, so statements about K0 are expressed
through structural relations rather than through the time-indexed operators listed here. Where the surrounding level is already
fixed, the notation suppresses that constant K-dependence only for brevity rather than to imply that thresholds, cycles, bound-
aries, axes, or continuumness are level-free. In those displayed signatures, bare M abbreviates the active Mx or Mx(t); A(t),
Θ(t), C(t), Ω(t), and ∂Ω(t) abbreviate A(K, t), Θ(K, t), C(K, t), Ω(K, t), and ∂Ω(K, t) for the fixed continuum under
discussion. The displayed signatures in this appendix are reader-facing projections of the exact operator definitions in Sec-
tion 11. They keep the principal output component visible while retaining the full coupled arguments needed by the formal
operator chapter. The K-level archive and the process atlas both use the glyph family (Ψ, Φ, Λ, U, X), but they do not share
one theorem-bearing namespace. In the K-level archive these glyphs are level-row shorthand; in the process atlas they are
process-layer operators local to the process modules. The list below is deliberately namespaced: it includes K-level glyphs, dy-
namic operators used in the formal chapters, and presentation aliases used only in specific rows. A glyph entry is therefore not
a global definition unless its entry explicitly says so. Bare Ψ denotes the generic birth/rebirth operator family of the formal
core. Its indexed forms state the route being used: Ψx→x+1 denotes adjacent-level birth, while a rebirth route may use a same-
level or cross-level candidate K ′ as specified by the local rebirth predicate. Legacy or local process uses must carry their level
or module subscript. The source K0 archive uses (Ψ0, Φ0, Λ0) as its local root process glyphs for distinction generation, rela-
tional reconfiguration, and compositional assembly. The unified synthesis also uses compact aliases such as F0, Q0, and U0
inside its K0 numeric rows; those aliases name local root constraints only and do not inherit the time-indexed K1+ dynamic
operator meanings listed below.
Eevol Structural evolution operator, often written locally as E after the chapter has bound the symbol: Eevol : K(t) !
K(t + dt). The decorated form avoids collision with energy quantities such as E(Kx).
F Flow operator: F : (J(t), P (t), A(t), Θ(t), M) 7! J(t + dt).
G Potential operator: G : (P (t), A(t), J(t), Θ(t), M) 7! P (t + dt).
Hthr Threshold-evolution operator, often written locally as H after the chapter has bound the symbol: Hthr :
(Θ(t), P (t), J(t), M) 7! Θ(t + dt).
Q Cycle operator: Q : (C(t), P (t), J(t), Θ(t)) 7! C(t + dt).
R Boundary operator: R : (∂Ω(t), P (t), J(t), Θ(t), M) 7! ∂Ω(t + dt).
Saxis Axis-structure operator, often written locally as S after the chapter has bound the symbol: Saxis :
(A(t), P (t), J(t), Θ(t), M) 7! A(t + dt). The decorated form avoids collision with scalar complexity S(K).
U Continuumness operator: U : (k(t), Ω(t), A(t), P (t), J(t), Θ(t), C(t), ∂Ω(t), M) 7! k(t + dt).
137
DoF(X) Degrees of freedom available to the continuum, level, or embedding object X in the local compatibility test. The
K0 synthesis rows use DoF (Kx)/DoF(Mx) as a dimensionless meta-space compatibility ratio.
Cnt Non-trivial lawful-cycle presence count or indicator in the local synthesis row. The threshold Cnt  1 means that at least
one non-trivial lawful cycle remains available to the tested structure.
Ψ0, Φ0, Λ0 Local K0 root process glyphs used in the source K0 archive for distinction generation, relational reconfiguration,
and compositional assembly.
Φ Meta-space evolution operator used in the K-level archive when a level’s embedding space is itself allowed to change.
Λ Constraint operator enforcing the active law or admissibility family in the relevant meta-domain.
X Logical-branching operator used when the formal branch structure of a continuum must be tracked explicitly. This is the
K-level archive convention; process modules that use X for collapse define that use locally.
Ψx→x+1 Birth operator for x 2 f 0, . . . ,11g: admissible transition (Kx, Mx) 7! (Kx+1, Mx+1) when the surrounding
birth, embedding, and threshold conditions are satisfied.
Ψx→y Non-adjacent birth-route notation for y > x . It is not an additional primitive unless a local theorem explicitly declares
it so; by default it abbreviates the admissible composition Ψy−1→y      Ψx→x+1, with every intermediate threshold
and embedding obligation still required.
Ψreb Rebirth-route operator family. A candidate- specific use is written Ψreb(K, K′, h; Rres(K), M, M′): Rres(K) is the
residue set of the collapsed continuum, M and M′ are the source and target embedding spaces, h : M ! M ′ is the
witness map, and the later candidate K ′ is tested against residue, threshold conditions, and identity conditions. This
notation allows same-level rebirth as well as cross-level rebirth when the local Definition 12.6 route permits it.
Eint Interaction operator for multiple continua.
A.4 Levels and Embedding Spaces
The labels below are mnemonic descriptions for quick notation lookup. The canonical level doctrine is stated in Section 10
and the generated K-level archive.
K0 Structural substrate (no time, no geometry, no energy).
K1 One–dimensional classical continua.
K2 Physical continua (fields, phases, percolation, Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless (BKT) transitions, mass–related struc-
tures).
K3 Chemical continua (reaction networks, reflexively autocatalytic and food-generated (RAF) closure).
K4 Protocellular continua (membranes, gradients, osmotic and curvature thresholds).
K5 Early neural and bioelectrical continua (ion channels, excitability, spikes).
K6 Cognitive continua (representations, binding, prediction).
K7 Social continua (norms, institutions, trust).
K8 Civilizational continua (infrastructures, systemic thresholds).
K9 Theory-level continua: theories, paradigms, ontologies, and formal languages treated as structured objects.
K10 Meta-theoretical continua: model-of-models recursion and self-referential theory structure.
K11 Evolving meta-theoretical spaces: operator and model-space evolution above local meta-model recursion.
K12 Global coherence layer: cross-framework compatibility, integrability, and the admissible upper envelope of the public
hierarchy.
A.5 Miscellaneous Symbols
dim(X) General structural dimension convention for any object X that is already represented as an axis set, structural set, or
locally linearized space in the surrounding argument.
dim(K) For K1 and above, the dimensionality of continuum K, fixed in this monograph as dim (K) = jA(K)j, where A(K)
is its effective axis set.
dim(K(t)) Time-slice dimensionality convention for an evolving continuum: dim (K(t)) = jA(K, t)j, where A(K, t) is the
effective axis set at that slice.
dimcov(Ω(K)) Covering dimension of Ω(K) with the subspace topology inherited from the declared ambient space. This
notation is used only for nonempty admissible regions unless a local empty-set convention is explicitly declared.
dimeff(Ω(K)) Effective admissible-state dimension used in cross-level emergence comparisons. It may coincide with
dimcov(Ω(K)) only under the local hypotheses stated in the surrounding argument; otherwise it is a rank or active-axis
proxy, not the literal covering dimension. Legacy displays of dim (Ω(K1)) < dim(Ω(K2)) in transition schematics
are to be read as dim eff-comparisons. Local linearized approximations may also use a separate symbol such as rlin(K).
138
dim(S, ∆, C) Dimension of a structural tuple, read as the dimension of the structural set equipped with its declared difference
and connectivity data.
dim(K0) Base-level dimension convention for the structural substrate: dim (K0) = 0 , because K0 carries distinguishability
without a geometric axis family of the higher-level kind. Abstract K0 structural variation in A(K0) is therefore not
counted by the higher-level effective-axis dimension dim(K).
rlin(K) Optional local linearized rank notion for a section-specific approximation. It is introduced separately whenever a
local argument needs a rank concept distinct from dim (K).
Cmax(t) Maximal compatible cycle set at the time slice used by the operator chapter’s death criterion.
Cmax(K) Maximal structurally stable cycle complex or set associated with K under the full threshold landscape Θ(K).
Time-slice death checks use Cmax(t), and summary statistics must be named separately.
spanstr(A) Structural span of a set of axes: the smallest structurally closed subobject, inside the fixed ambient continuum or
meta-space, that contains A and is closed under the locally declared admissible composition, restriction, and threshold-
respecting transport operations. Equivalently it is the intersection of all locally declared structurally closed subobjects
that contain A. This notation is used only in contexts where that local closed-subobject family is nonempty and stable
under arbitrary intersections; otherwise the section must declare a replacement span operation.
spanlin(A) Ordinary linear span of a set of axes inside a local linearization. It is used only when a section states an explicit
linear approximation.
span(A) Shorthand for span str(A) in theorem-bearing structural text unless a section explicitly declares a local linearisation.
Use spanlin(A) only under such an explicit linear approximation. The subscripted forms remain preferred.
χΩ(s; K, t) Binary admissibility indicator with codomain f0, 1g: χΩ(s; K, t) = 1 exactly when the state s of K at
time t lies in Ω(K, t), and χΩ(s; K, t) = 0 otherwise. The symbol χΩ is reserved for pointwise membership; use
1{Ω(K,t)̸=∅} for nonemptiness of the admissible region itself.
This notation appendix is intentionally compact; more specialised symbols used only in particular extension papers are de-
fined locally in those texts.

C.3 Vertical Continuity Conditions
For neighbouring levels Kx and Kx+1 the following continuity conditions hold:
• State spaces are nested via projection: there exists a projection πx+1→x : Ω(Kx+1) ! Ω(Kx) that forgets the new axis.
• Axes are monotonic: A(Kx)  A(Kx+1) and dim A(Kx+1) > dim A(Kx).
• Thresholds respect inheritance: thresholds of Kx are recovered from those of Kx+1 by restricting to the subspace where
the new axis is fixed.

D Core 1.3 Source-Audit Appendix
This appendix records the principles by which the 1.3 release remains source-first while still operating as
a publication program rather than as a static archive.
D.1 Why an appendix is still needed
The main body of the monograph is written to be read. The source-audit machinery is written to be
checked. Those are related but non-identical tasks. If the full provenance burden were pushed into the
146
Table 40: Parameters governing meta-theoretical landscapes at K11.

main body, the book would become harder to read. If it were omitted entirely, the reader would need
to trust a hidden workflow. The appendix therefore carries the discipline without replacing the main
narrative.
D.2 Witness classes
The release uses several witness classes:
• the public LaTeX corpus as the source-native textual witness,
• the archival compiled PDF as the stable page-and-line witness,
• the bounded journal-core extraction as the outward review-focused derivative witness,
• and companion packets as support witnesses for chronology, theorem fate, and release packaging.
None of these witnesses should be mistaken for the others. The source witness is not the same as the
release manifest. The release manifest is not the same as the theorem. The journal-core article is not the
same as the monograph. The 1.3 publication line remains healthy only when these roles stay distinct.
D.3 Questions that the appendix answers
This appendix is meant to answer concrete review questions.
• From which public source stack is the present volume built?
• Which outward article is derived from it?
• Why is the monograph larger than the journal-core article?
• What justifies calling the volume 1.3 rather than simply republishing 1.2?
• How should later ESTRA and channel projections interpret the distinction between formal master,
review article, and support packet?
The release is stronger when those questions can be answered inside the volume rather than by pointing
the reader to an unrelated dashboard.
147
D.4 Current boundary
Core 1.3 should therefore be read as a source-first enlargement and clarification of the formal publication
shell. The monograph does not pretend that every future projection is already proved. The journal core
does not pretend to be the whole theory. The companion packets do not pretend to be the manuscript.
That three-way distinction is the governing boundary of the current release.
E Journal-Core Extraction Bridge
This appendix explains how the journal-core article relates to the master monograph.
E.1 Why the journal-core exists
Some channels require a bounded, faster-reading scientific artifact. Editors, reviewers, and external read-
ers often need a paper-sized object whose defended claim can be read in one sitting. The journal-core
exists for that purpose. Its job is not to replace the monograph but to provide a narrow article that remains
anchored to the same scientific truth conditions.
E.2 What the journal-core may omit
The journal-core may compress:
• extensive chapter-scale didactic explanation,
• large parts of the domain atlas,
• broad module coverage,
• detailed appendical inventories,
• and some of the monograph-level pedagogical scaffolding.
It may not silently change:
• theorem scope,
• explicit nonclaims,
• claimed source basis,
• figure meaning,
• or the relation between inherited corpus and present defended claim.
E.3 What the monograph guarantees to later artifacts
Because the journal-core is extracted from the present volume, later owner-facing and public channels do
not need to improvise their own understanding of the science. They can derive from the master monograph
when they need depth, from the journal core when they need bounded exposition, and from the companion
layer when they need support evidence.
This is the practical publication value of the monograph. It is not merely larger than the article. It is
the document that prevents every later projection from becoming a separate interpretive exercise.

F.3 Compact reading order by reviewer role
Rapid critical reviewer. Read the abstract, theorem roadmap, relevant theorems and corollaries, the
worked examples, and the journal-core bridge appendix. Return to this matrix only to choose a new route
after that first pass. This route should reveal immediately whether the release is too large, too narrow, or
too broad in scope.
Formal mathematical reviewer. Read the model, results, axioms, operators, collapse/rebirth material,
hierarchy chapter, notation appendix, and source-audit chapter. The decisive question is whether the
derived bounded claim can be reconstructed from the stated source-native rows without informal supple-
mentation.
Generalist scientific reviewer. Read the introduction, reader guide, theorem roadmap, worked exam-
ples, discussion, conclusion, and then return to the formal chapters selectively. The decisive question here
is whether the volume explains itself honestly enough that scientific judgment can precede local notation
mastery.

G External Criticism Reaction and Scientific Closure
This appendix records the evidence-first terminal reaction to the Stanislav Tsukrov external review pack-
age for OC Core 1.3.3. A criticism item is not closed merely because a response paragraph exists. It
is closed only when the weakness is answered by manuscript/release repair, source-tradition evidence,
replay evidence, theorem-fate discipline, tuple/K rigor evidence, or an owner-gated owner-review-gated
boundary. No 1.3.3 blocker is closed by lowering a claim.
G.1 Closure invariant
For substantive criticism, closure requires a concrete delta: source-tradition repair, theorem-fate evidence,
prediction protocol boundary, tuple role table, K-level falsifier criteria, replay evidence, release-packet
update, or public acknowledgement entry. Reviewer source material remains private and no canonical
claim is promoted by this appendix.

G.3 Prediction and theorem evidence boundaries
Prediction language is tiered by evidence. OC may state structural signatures and diagnostic classifiers
where operators and observables are declared. It may state quantitative held-out predictions only where
protocol, data/code route, formula or executable procedure, output, comparator, and falsifier are present.
Legacy master-theorem labels are not promoted by label alone; only dependency-checked rows such as
the bounded Theorem A route carry theorem force.
G.4 Tuple and hierarchy limits
The tuple is treated as an interface with primitive and derived roles. Minimality, completeness, exact
K-level necessity, and higher-order functional promotion are release-bounded until their proof gates pass.
The current release is closed by evidence rows, replay gates, theorem-fate discipline, and explicit exten-
sion boundaries, not by pretending unfinished proofs have been solved and not by lowering a claim as a
closure mechanism.
G.5 Reviewer acknowledgement
Stanislav Tsukrov is acknowledged as a substantive external reviewer whose criticism changed release
wording, source-tradition routing, theorem/prediction evidence boundaries, and response automation.
This acknowledgement is not an endorsement and does not authorize outbound sending.

P.1 Extended modules and cross-level structures
The ontology of continua is organised as a hierarchical sequence of levels
K0;K 1;:::;K 12;
each representing a qualitatively distinct form of structure, dynamics, and admissible states. Every level
Kx possesses:
• a state space Ω(Kx),
• a set of axes A(Kx),
• potentialsP (Kx),
• thresholds Θ(Kx),
• flowsJ(Kx),
• cyclesC(Kx) with characteristic times  (Kx),
• a continuum measure k(Kx),
• and a boundary @Ω(Kx) describing the conditions of collapse or transition.
EachKx is embedded into a corresponding meta-space Mx that determines the admissible axes and
states:
A(Kx) A(Mx); Ω(Kx)  Ω(Mx):
The meta-space restricts the degrees of freedom available to the continuum and thereby shapes its evolu-
tion.
P.1.1 Dimensional Growth and Transitions Kx !Kx+1
A transition from level Kx toKx+1 occurs when:
1. a new class of differences emerges that cannot be represented within the existing axes A(Kx);
2. structural tension exceeds a threshold:
T (Kx)> Θdim(Kx);
3. the meta-space requires a higher-dimensional representation;
4. the existing configuration space Ω(Kx) becomes insuﬀicient or collapses onto its boundary
@Ω(Kx).
This process is irreversible:
dimKx+1  dimKx;
and any “reduction” of dimensionality corresponds to the death of the continuum:
Ω(Kx) = ∅:
188
P.1.2 Universal Structure Across All Levels
Despite the qualitative diversity of levels, every Kx shares a common formal structure. The evolution of
a continuum is governed by:
Kx(t +dt) = E
␀
Kx(t);M x(t)

;
whereE is an evolution operator constrained by the meta-space Mx. A continuum evolves only within
the admissible region of its meta-space:
Kx(t +dt) 2 Ω(Mx) or the evolution is forbidden:
The continuum measure is:
k(Kx) = kΩ kA kC kJ kT;
where:
• kΩ measures the volume of allowed states,
• kA counts realised axes relative to the meta-space,
• kC reflects stability of cycles,
• kJ describes coherence of flows,
• kT measures structural tension relative to thresholds.
P.1.3 Hierarchy of Levels K0 !K12
Each level represents a distinct stratum of organisation:
• K0 — meta-pressure, possibility conditions, and pre-structural logic;
• K1 — continuous one-dimensional continua;
• K2 — two-dimensional continua with internal flows and clusters;
• K3 — chemical configuration spaces and reaction manifolds;
• K4 — protocell-level continua with membranes and boundaries;
• K5 — neural continua with excitation cycles and attractors;
• K6 — cognitive continua with predictive models;
• K7 — social continua with group-level stability cycles;
• K8 — civilisational continua with large-scale coordination flows;
• K9 — theoretical continua (structure of explanations);
• K10 — meta-theoretical continua (structure of structural spaces);
• K11 — formal ontologies and logic-level continua;
• K12 — meta-ontological continua governing the possibility space of all lower levels.
Higher levels do not replace lower ones; they embed and extend them:
Kx Mx; M x  Ω(Kx+1):

P.1.4 Boundaries, Collapse and Death of Continua
EveryKx has a boundary @Ω(Kx) where the continuum loses admissibility. A continuum dies when:
Ω(Kx) = ∅ ) k(Kx) = 0;
which corresponds to:
• violation of thresholds Θ(Kx),
• loss of stable cycles C(Kx),
• destructive flows reaching critical values,
• collapse of axes or incompatibility with Mx.
Death is distinct from evolution: it removes the continuum from the space of admissible structures
and cannot be undone.
P.1.5 Role of k-Level Structure in the Core Model
TheK-levels provide the vertical backbone of the Ontology of Continua. They:
• organise emergence from physical to cognitive to social to meta-ontological structures;
• define the recursionKx !Mx !Kx+1;
• supply the dimensional ladder necessary for universal applicability;
• constrain the evolution of continua via admissibility conditions;
• unify all domains of reality under one mathematical framework.
The structure ofK-levels makes the ontology both hierarchical and recursive: every level depends on
the meta-space above it and constrains the level below.
P.1.6 K0 Overview
LevelK0 represents the pre-structural foundation of all continua. It is not a physical or geometric domain
but the logical substrate that defines the conditions of possibility for any continuum Kx. It provides
the metapressure, admissibility constraints, logical superiority (Axiom 0.3), and the universal rules that
govern which structures may exist.
K0 does not itself possess the conventional axes or geometric dimensions. Instead, it specifies:
• the meta-laws L determining structural coherence,
• the possibility space P for all continua,
• the metapressure driving emergence of differences,
• the universal thresholds that define admissibility and collapse,
• the recursion rules Kx 7!Mx 7!Kx+1.
Its primary function is logical governance of all deeper levels.
P.1.7 State Space Ω(K0)
Ω(K0) consists of all admissible configurations of the pair
(P; L);
where P is the meta-domain of possible structures and L is the system of meta-laws that enforce coher-
ence.
Because K0 is pre-geometric, Ω(K0) is not a metric space but an abstract set with the following
properties:
190
1. Ω(K0) contains all possible specifications of structural constraints that allow continua to exist.
2. Ω(K0) has no internal topology unless induced by constraints in L.
3. Every Ω(Kx) forx  1 is a subset of Ω(K0):
Ω(Kx)  Ω(K0):
There is no continuous evolution inside Ω(K0); it defines conditions, not dynamical trajectories.
P.1.8 Boundary @Ω(K0)
The boundary of K0 consists of all meta-configurations that violate internal coherence conditions of the
meta-laws L.
A configuration (P; L) lies on@Ω(K0) if:
• the laws contradict each other,
• admissibility collapses (P becomes empty),
• recursion rules become undefined,
• structural consistency conditions cannot be maintained.
Crossing@Ω(K0) corresponds to the logical impossibility of any continuum.
P.1.9 Axes A(K0)
K0 has no geometric axes. Instead it contains:
• abstract axes of possibility,
• admissibility axes governing which structures can be produced,
• meta-axes that define the logical dependencies among levels.
In formal terms:
A(K0) = fdimensions of admissible structural variation g:
These are the ultimate sources of all later axes:
A(Kx) A(K0):
P.1.10 Potentials P (K0)
Potentials atK0 describe meta-conditions that push continua toward structure:
P (K0) = fpressures, constraints, logical gradients g:
They include:
• metapressure (Axiom 0.z),
• pressure toward structuralisation,
• pressure toward compatible differences,
• pressure toward nonempty admissible spaces.
These potentials are not numeric energies but logical intensities.
191
P.1.11 Thresholds Θ(K0)
Thresholds atK0 correspond to logical break-points:
Θ(K0) = fΘcoh; Θadm; Θmetag:
Examples:
• Θcoh: minimal coherence of meta-laws,
• Θadm: minimal non-empty possibility space,
• Θmeta: minimal support for recursion.
If any threshold is violated, no continuum can exist at any Kx.
P.1.12 Flows J(K0)
There are no physical flows at K0. J(K0) instead contains:
• flows of admissibility,
• flows of logical dependence,
• propagation of constraints,
• meta-flows describing which structures can generate others.
These flows shape the space of possible continua but do not correspond to time evolution.
P.1.13 Cycles C(K0)
Cycles atK0 correspond to:
• fixed-point consistency cycles,
• meta-stability loops of admissibility,
• self-referential closure cycles in L.
A cycle exists if:
Π(C)> Θcoh;
where Π(C) is the “power” of the meta-cycle (stability of recursive closure).
There are no temporal cycles; these are purely logical cycles.

Time does not exist at K0.
Theorem “Emergence of Time from C-cycles” (Physics Run):

Π(C)> Θtime:
Thus:
 (K0) undefined:

k(K0) = H(Ω(K0)) kA(K0) kcoh(K0);

P.1.22 Collapse and Death of K0

Ω(K0) = ∅:

P.1.23 Falsifiability of K0

Failure of any of these behaviours empirically falsifies K0.

P.1.26 K1 Overview

 .
The creation of K1 is the first step where:

• structural tension can propagate,
• constraints produce continuous curves.
Every higher continuum inherits A1 as its foundational axis.
P.1.27 State Space Ω(K1)
The state space of K1 is:
Ω(K1) = C0(X;V );
the space of continuous functions from the one-dimensional domain X to a value set V .
Properties:
1. Ω(K1) is infinite-dimensional (function space).
2. Every configuration is continuous by definition.
3. Discontinuities lie outside Ω(K1) and correspond to violations of structural coherence.
4. X may be open, closed, compact or non-compact depending on constraints in the corresponding
M1.
This is the minimal space in which continuous variation exists.

P.1.34 Time  (K1)

P.1.66 K3 Overview
K3 is the level at which chemical organisation becomes structurally possible. It represents the transition
from purely geometric and topological continua (K0–K2) to systems in which:
• reactions, transformations and conversions appear as admissible flows,
• potentials correspond to reaction aﬀinities and concentration gradients,
• boundaries@Ω include molecular-compositional and topological constraints,
• minimal autocatalytic closure becomes representable,
• the first structurally coherent networks arise (RAF networks).
The dimensional transition Ψ2→3 occurs when incompatible chemical differences cannot be expressed
within the axes fA1;A 2g of K2. A new axis A3 is introduced, representing a distinct dimension of
composition space, enabling emergent chemical continua.
K3 serves as the structural substrate for all later biological and cognitive continua, but itself remains
non-living.

P.1.106 K5 Overview
K5 is the level at which electrical excitability emerges as a new ontological dimension. The protocell
boundary of K4 becomes an electrically active membrane through the formation of ion channels with
controlled conductance. This generates a new axis:
Aexc : ∆V 7! electrical state difference;
where ∆V is the transmembrane potential.
This axis is not definable in K4. It represents a new class of incompatible differences and therefore
constitutes a genuine increase in dimension.
Organisationally,K5 is characterised by:
• stable ion channels (open/closed/leaky/blocked),
• controlled ionic fluxes,
• excitable cycles (excitation–recovery),
• refractory dynamics,
• noise control and thresholded responses,
• self-sustaining electrical organisation tightly coupled to the chemical interior.
K5 is the minimal neuron-like continuum, even if no real neurons exist yet.

• Popen — open probabilities,

• x(t) — internal activation variables,

P.1.126 K6 Overview
K6 is the level at which cognitive organisation emerges as an ontological dimension. The excitable
electrical dynamics of K5 produce stable attractors; these attractors become models that encode internal
structure, memory, predictive states and representational relations.
The birth ofK6 occurs when excitation cycles ofK5 are no longer merely electrical waves, but become
informationally interpretable patterns whose differences cannot be expressed inA(K5). This necessitates
a new set of axes and a new dimensional structure.
The minimal features:
• representational states,
• prediction capability (prediction error axis),
• semantic and binding structure,
• internal modelst,
• memory consolidation/reconsolidation,
• stable components of cognitive graphs,
• emergence of proto-symbols.
K6 is the smallest continuum that deserves the name “cognitive”. It is not yet linguistic or social
(those belong to K7).

• x(t) — activation patterns inherited from K5 attractors,
• ri — representational units (proto-symbols),
• PE t — prediction error,
• Bt — binding configuration,
• Mcon,Mrec — consolidated vs. reconsolidating memory states.
Admissibility:
D(m)  Θcog; jPE tj< Θpred; B t 2 binding-capacity:
D(m) is inconsistency of model m.

P.3 Cross-level structures
P.3.1 Purpose of the Cross-K layer
The Cross-K layer formalises all structures, transitions and constraints that link different continuum levels
K0 !K12. While eachK-level has its own ontology (axes, potentials, thresholds, flows, cycles, domains
Ω(K), boundaries@Ω(K) and continuum measurek(K)), many phenomena in the Core requirerelations
across levels. These relations are neither optional nor external: they are part of the intrinsic architecture
of a dynamic continuum.
The Cross-K layer therefore:
• defines mapping structures between levels;
• specifies transition operators and their constraints;
• introduces consistency conditions ensuring that evolution across adjacent levels is mathematically
and conceptually valid;
• provides global landscape rules , describing how the entire stack of K-levels forms a coherent meta-
continuum.
P.3.2 Definition of Cross-K structures
A Cross-K structure is any formal object that:
1. involves at least two levelsKi;K j withi 6=j;
2. establishes a relation Rij between their components (A;P; Θ;J;C; Ω;@ Ω;k );
3. satisfies the general compatibility rule:
Rij :Ki $Kj
while preserving continuity and allowing valid transitions under the global operator E.
Thus Cross-K structures include:
• transition maps (dimensional, structural, energetic);
• inheritance relations (axes, potentials, thresholds);
• boundary transformations between@Ω(Ki) and@Ω(Kj);
• cycle projections and lifts (mapping cycles from one level into another);
• global constraints ensuring that no level violates the rules of its neighbours.
298
P.3.3 Role of this master file
This master module intentionally remains a thin orchestration layer. It does not store heavy theoretical
content. Instead, it:
• introduces the concept of Cross-K structures,
• provides the global definition and purpose,
• and assembles all detailed cross-level analyses through \input.
The individual transition sections are organised as:
• global landscape (all-level perspective),
• local transitions (Ki !Ki+1),
• special two-way or non-adjacent mappings where required.
P.3.4 Module structure
The following files are orchestrated by this module:
• crossk_global_landscape.tex — global multi-level geometry;
• crossk_k0_k1.tex, crossk_k1_k2.tex, …— adjacent-level transition blocks;
• crossk_k10_k11.tex, crossk_k11_k12.tex — upper-level transitions and meta-structures.
P.3.5 Inclusion of detailed sections
The detailed cross-K analyses can be included as:
\input{content/crossk/crossk_global_landscape.tex}
\input{content/crossk/crossk_k0_k1.tex}
\input{content/crossk/crossk_k1_k2.tex}

This file thus defines the conceptual container for the Cross-K domain of OC Core 1.3.
P.3.6 Global cross-K landscape
The cross-K landscape describes how individual continua Kd are embedded into a single multi-level
structure. Instead of treating each level as an isolated theory, the Ontology of Continua organises them
as a chain of dimension-increasing transitions:
Rd :Kd !Kd+1;
where eachRd is a constrained transition that:
• preserves the core axioms (non-emptiness of Ω, thresholds, flows, cycles),
• introduces at least one new axis Anew 2Md nA(Kd),
• passes a dimensional threshold Td> Θd,dim,
• produces a strictly richer space of admissible states Ω(Kd+1)  Ω(Kd).
The global landscape is therefore not a flat list of levels, but a structured sequence of phase transitions
in which eachKd emerges from a predecessor and constrains its successors.
299
P.3.7 1. Levels involved and their roles
At a coarse resolution, the chain can be grouped into four bands:
1. Physical band (K0–K2): basic structure, action and percolation of connectivity.
2. Material and biological band (K3–K5): fields, chemistry, compartments and proto-neural dy-
namics.
3. Cognitive and social band (K6–K8): meaning, social systems and civilisational infrastructures.
4. Theoretical band (K9–K11): theories, metatheories and trans-metatheoretical constraints.
Each band is internally coherent but also linked by explicit cross-level operators Rd and by shared
meta-spacesMn.
P.3.8 2. Shared axes and thresholds across levels
Across the chainK0–K11, several structural motifs reappear:
• AxesA(Kd): each level introduces new axes but inherits transformed versions of earlier ones (e.g.
energy, gradients, information, roles, symbols).
• Thresholds Θ(Kd): existence, stability, critical, death and dimensional thresholds appear at all levels,
specialised to the local physics/biology/social/theoretical context.
• State domains Ω(Kd): every continuum has a non-empty domain of admissible states, with a bound-
ary@Ω(Kd) defined by violated thresholds.
• CyclesC(Kd): minimal stabilising cycles exist on each level (from trivial physical cycles to institu-
tional and meta-theoretical cycles).
The global landscape can be seen as the evolution of these structural motifs as dimension and com-
plexity increase.
P.3.9 3. Cross-level flows, cycles, and tensions
Cross-level dynamics can be summarised by three families of objects:
Flows. Cross-level flows Jd,d+1 map states and structures from Kd to Kd+1 (e.g. chemical gradients
shapingK4, neural patterns inducing K6, social norms supporting K8).
Cycles. Some cycles explicitly span multiple levels, such as civilisation–theory feedback loops (K8–K9–
K8) or meta-theory–practice cycles (K9–K10–K8).
Tension. Cross-level tensionTd,d+1 measures mismatch between the constraints ofKd andKd+1; exces-
sive tension can prevent the birth of a new level or trigger collapse downwards.
Formally, one can write a generic cross-level tension functional
Td,d+1 =F
␀
A(Kd+1) ␀A(Kd); P(Kd+1) ␀P (Kd); Jd,d+1; Θ(Kd+1) ␀ Θ(Kd)

withTd,d+1> Θd,dim signalling a dimensional transition.

P.3.10 4. Birth and death conditions in the global chain
Birth of a new level Kd+1 is governed by three conditions:
1. Availability of a new axis: there existsAnew 2Md such thatAnew /2A(Kd).
2. Dimensional tension: structural tension exceeds a critical threshold, Td> Θd,dim, making the old
configuration unstable without a new dimension.
3. Admissible state extension: the new domain satisfies Ω(Kd+1) 6= ∅ and Ω(Kd+1)  Ω(Kd).
Death of a level Kd may occur locally (collapse of a specific continuum) or globally (destruction of

P.3.11 5. Canonical cross-level chains
Several cross-level chains are of particular importance:
• Physical–chemical–biological chain: K1 !K2 !K3 !K4 !K5 (from action and percolation
to membranes and proto-neural dynamics).
• Biological–cognitive–social chain:K4 !K5 !K6 !K7 (from gradients and spikes to cognition
and institutions).
• Social–civilisational–theoretical chain: K7 ! K8 ! K9 ! K10 ! K11 (from norms and roles
to civilisational technologies and meta-frameworks).
The detailed cross-K modules in the technical derivation atlas refine these canonical chains by provid-

transition.
In this sense, the global cross-K landscape is the map of how all individual continua Kd fit into a
single, coherent, multi-level structure.

The transition fromK0 toK1 represents the first and most fundamental cross-level structure in the entire

threshold conditions for the emergence of K1.

P.3.30 K3–K4 cross-level structure
The transitionK3 !K4 marks the emergence of the biological continuum from the chemical continuum.
WhileK3 supports chemical connectivity, reaction pathways and stable clusters, K4 introduces:
• membranes and boundary formation,
• sustained gradients (ion, pH, concentration, redox),
• osmotic and electrochemical potentials,
• active and passive transport flows,
• metabolic cycles and buffering loops,
• early information carriers (charge, structure, templating),
• regulatory thresholds and proto-homeostasis.
This is the birth of the first living-like continua: systems capable of maintaining non-equilibrium
structure.

P.4 Cycle Structure in the Ontology of Continua
This master section provides the unified formal framework for cycle structure in the Ontology of Continua
(OC). Cycles constitute the central mechanism of structural persistence: a continuum remains alive if and
only if it maintains at least one structurally stable cycle that stays within its admissible state space Ω(K)
and maintains positive continuumness k(K;t ). The material below consolidates all general results on
cycles across levelsK0–K12, independent of domain-specific interpretations.
P.4.1 Definition of Cycles
A cycle of a continuum K is a closed trajectory
C : [0; ] ! Ω(K); C (0) = C( );
such that:
1. C(t) remains strictly inside the admissible domain: dist (C(t);@ Ω(K))> 0;
2. the flow fieldJ(t) supports the trajectory: ˙C(t) = J

3. the cycle forms a stable attractor under the evolution operator E :K(t) !K(t +dt).
A cycle is structurally stable if perturbations of potentials, flows or thresholds do not destroy its
closed form: there exists " > 0 such that all trajectories with initial distance < " return to the cycle
within bounded time.
329
P.4.2 Role of Cycles in Continuum Persistence
In OC, cycles are not dynamical ornaments but structural necessities. They serve several essential func-
tions:
• Maintain distance from the boundary@Ω(K). Without stable cycles, trajectories generically reach
the boundary, where thresholds saturate and the continuum collapses.
• Stabilise potentials and flows. Cycles maintain oscillatory, periodic, quasi-periodic or recurrent
regimes that preserve the structural viability of K.
• Carry the measure of continuumness. The contribution of cycles enters explicitly into the global
measurek(K;t ) through their stability, diversity and distance to @Ω(K).
• Ensure structural identity. The presence of characteristic cycle complexes allows a continuum to
preserve its structural type across time.
As a consequence, the disappearance of all structurally stable cycles coincides with the death of the
continuum.
P.4.3 Cycle Complexes
For most continua, cycles do not appear in isolation but in interconnected clusters called cycle complexes.
A cycle complexCcx is a finite or countably infinite collection of cycles fCig satisfying:
1. shared supporting flows;
2. structural compatibility under perturbations of thresholds;
3. existence of transition paths between cycles that do not reach @Ω(K).
The maximal cycle complexCmax(K) is the set of all cycles that remain stable under the full threshold
landscape Θ(K).
Theorem 7 (OC Core) states that
Cmax(K) = ; ( ) Ω(K) = ;;
i.e. death is equivalent to the disappearance of the maximal cycle complex.

P.4.6 Cycles Across the K-Hierarchy
Cycles appear at every level of the continuum hierarchy, though their interpretations differ:
• K1: periodic field or geometric oscillations.
• K2: coherence cycles, topological defects, phase loops.
• K3: catalytic cycles in RAF networks.
• K4: metabolic and membrane-maintenance cycles.
• K5: excitation–repolarisation cycles (proto-spikes).
• K6: cognitive feedback loops and prediction cycles.
• K7: institutional cycles and cooperation loops.
• K8: infrastructural and energy-logistics cycles.
• K9;K 10: theoretical and meta-theoretical cycles.
Despite these differences, all such cycles share: closure inside Ω(K), positive distance to @Ω, and
stabilising interaction with thresholds.
P.4.7 Cycles and Dimensional Transitions
Dimensional birth (Kx ! Kx+1) requires that cycles at level Kx approach the dimensional threshold
Θdim(Kx) in such a way that their representational capacity becomes insuﬀicient. Loss of cycle stability
is one of the earliest indicators of an impending dimensional transition.
P.4.8 Summary
Cycles encode the persistence, identity and structural viability of continua across all domains. Their
stability, diversity and organisation form a key component of continuumnessk(K;t ). The disappearance
of all structurally stable cycles corresponds to the death of a continuum, while deformation and emergence
of new cycles signal structural reorganisation or dimensional transition.
331
P.4.9 Cycles on K0
LevelK0 represents the meta-ontological background of the Ontology of Continua. It possesses no ge-
ometry, no time, no admissible state space in the sense of Ω(K), no flows J, no thresholds Θ, and no
operators of evolution. For this reason, the notion of a cycle cannot be defined on K0.
P.4.10 Absence of State Space and Time
Cycles require:
1. a non-empty state space Ω(K);
2. a notion of time or parametrisation t 2 [0; ];
3. a flow fieldJ generating closed trajectories.
None of these structures exist on K0. Formally:
Ω(K0) = ;; @ Ω(K0) undefined; J K0 undefined;
and no parameter t exists that could index a trajectory.
Therefore, a cycle
C : [0; ] ! Ω(K); C (0) = C( );
cannot be formulated.
P.4.11 Structural Reason
LevelK0 is not a continuum but a logical condition of possibility for continua of levels K1 and above.
It establishes no dynamical or geometric structure from which cycles could emerge. All cycle-related
notions—length, stability, distance to boundary, cycle complexes, or contributions to continuumness—
are strictly inapplicable.
P.4.12 Implication for Higher Levels
The absence of cycles on K0 implies:
• the concept of time  (K) begins only atK1, where a continuous axis is first defined;
• the first non-trivial cycles appear at K1 as trivial or degenerate oscillatory structures of a one-
dimensional field;
• structural cycles in the full sense (stability, distance to @Ω, interaction with thresholds) emerge only
at levelsK2 and above;
• the birth of cycles is itself a signature of the phase transition K0 !K1.
P.4.13 Summary
No cycles exist on K0. Cycle structure becomes meaningful only beginning with K1, where time, state
space and flows first appear. Accordingly, the file cycles_k0.tex records a formal non-existence
statement, required for the internal consistency of the cycle taxonomy across the entire hierarchy of con-
tinua.

P.5 Structural Jets
The jet formalism introduced in this section provides a unified, dimension-agnostic description ofinfinites-
imal structural propagation across all continua in the Ontology of Continua (OC). While the operators E,
Ψ, Φ andU describe macroscopic evolution, embedding, deformation of admissible regions and global
continuumness, the jet hierarchy captures the local differential structure governing how continua deform
along their axes, potentials, flows, thresholds, and boundary gradients.
In classical mathematics, jets represent truncated Taylor expansions of smooth functions. In OC, jets
generalise this idea: a jet is a local, structurally admissible fragment of continuum evolution, encoding
all allowed derivatives of all structural components up to a specified order. This includes derivatives of:
• axesA(t) and their deformation modes,
• potentialsP (t) and their gradients @P /@A,
• thresholds Θ(t) and their rate of change,
• flowsJ(t), including cross-level flows and boundary exchange,
• cyclesC(t) and their infinitesimal stability conditions,
• admissible regions Ω(K) and their boundary geometry @Ω(K),
• continuumnessk(t) and its differential response.
Thus, a jet represents the infinitesimal content of the universal evolution operator:
E(K(t);M (t)) = K(t + ∆t);
providing a differential expansion that allows OC to connect macroscopic evolution to local geometric
constraints.

P.5.6 Jets on K0
The levelK0 represents the degenerate, pre-geometric continuum of the Ontology of Continua (OC). It
contains no axes, no potentials, no thresholds beyond the minimal existence threshold Θ0 =" >0, and
no temporal evolution. Consequently, the jet structure on K0 is both trivial and foundational: it provides
the limiting case against which all higher-order jets are defined.
Formally, the structural content of K0 is given by:
K0 = (S; ∆; C);
where S is an undifferentiated structural substrate, ∆ is the minimal distinction required for the exis-
tence of a continuum, and C denotes the admissible compositions of distinctions. No metric, topological,
temporal, or dynamical structure exists at this level.
ThusK0 admits only the zero jet, representing the fact that no derivatives of any structural quantity
can be defined.
P.5.7 Definition of Jets on K0
SinceK0 possesses no time parameter, no axes, and no dynamical fields, the general definition of n-jets
collapses to the trivial object:
J n(K0) = f0g for alln  0:
This means:
• no quantities can vary with time (time does not yet exist),
• no gradients can be defined (no axes exist),
• no flows can be defined (no admissible transitions),
• no thresholds evolve (only the existence threshold Θ0),
• @Ω(K0) is static and degenerate.
The jet formalism therefore records the essential fact that K0 exhibits zero differential structure. All
higher jet structures J n(Kx) forx  1 must reduce to J n(K0) in the appropriate singular limit.

T0< Θ0 =":

K0 = ∅:

minimal consistency condition of the pre-continuum. Any attempt to introduce derivative-like behaviour
would violate admissibility, since no such behaviour is defined.

P.5.10 Summary
Jets onK0 are trivial but foundational:
• all jets reduce to the zero jet,

P.8 Master Theorems of Core 1.2

P.8.1 Representability Theorems for Levels K2,K4,K8
Theorem 1 (Representability of K2). Any Level-K2 system described by local fields, threshold inter-
actions, and quantized excitations can be represented as a continuum
K2 = (Ω 2;@ Ω2;A 2;P 2; Θ2;J 2;C 2; (K2);k 2)
satisfying the axioms of Core 1.2.
Proof sketch. Local fields and their excitations define axes A2; threshold interactions are encoded
in Θ2; admissible field configurations form Ω2; the field dynamics induce flows J2 and cycles C2 (e.g.
periodic or quasi-periodic configurations). By construction, the structural tuple satisfies Axioms K.1–
K.7. The joint evolution operator E can be chosen to coincide with the local field dynamics, ensuring
compatibility with the Level-0 axioms and preserving admissibility in Ω(M ).
Theorem 2 (Representability ofK4). Any autocatalytic chemical system with closed metabolic cycles
and a stable boundary can be represented as a continuum K4.
Proof sketch. Concentrations and reaction configurations span Ω4; the membrane or compartment
defines the boundary @Ω4; stoichiometric directions define axes A4; chemical potentials provide P4;
kinetic constraints (e.g. saturation, inhibition, energetics) define thresholds Θ4; material fluxes define
flowsJ4; metabolic cycles correspond to cyclesC4. As long as at least one cycle closes and the boundary
prevents uncontrolled leakage, we obtaink4> 0. All structural elements map directly to the axioms of a
continuum, soK4 satisfies Core 1.2.
469
Theorem 3 (Representability of K8). Any civilizational–technological system with stable infrastruc-
ture, norms, and information flows can be represented as a continuum K8.
Proof sketch. Agents and their states form Ω8; inter-system boundaries (political, economic, infras-
tructural) define @Ω8; technological and symbolic codes define axes A8; resources and indicators (en-
ergy, capital, capacity, knowledge) define potentialsP8; institutional and technological constraints define
thresholds Θ8; material and informational streams define flows J8; institutional and infrastructural feed-
back loops define cycles C8. If the underlying interaction graph is connected enough and key cycles are
sustained, thenk8> 0. Thus the system is representable as a continuum of Level K8.
P.8.2 Compatibility Theorem K $M
Theorem 4 (Necessary and suﬀicient conditions for compatibility K $ M ). A continuum K can
evolve under the joint operator E without destruction if and only if the following conditions hold:
1. Ω(K)  Ω(M );
2. A(K) A(M );
3. thresholds Θ are refinements of the environmental thresholds ΘM ;
4. the dynamicsE are consistent with the meta-domain evolution Φ.
Proof sketch. Necessity: violation of (1) drives the trajectory K(t) outside Ω(M ); violation of (2) or
(3) leads to axes or thresholds unsupported by the meta-domain, violating Axioms 0.2, 0.6, and Φ:2. In
each case, Axioms D.1–D.3 imply that either Ω becomes empty or death thresholds are crossed. Suﬀi-
ciency: if (1)–(4) hold, then trajectories generated by E remain inside Ω(M ), with thresholds compatible
by design. No forced violation of death thresholds occurs, so destruction is not imposed by the environ-
ment.
P.8.3 Theorem on Impossibility of Evolution Outside M
Theorem 5 (Impossibility of evolution outside the meta-domain). LetK  M be a continuum sat-
isfying the axioms of Core 1.2. If there exists a time t∗ and a state s∗ /2 Ω(M ), then there is no valid
evolution operatorE that extends the evolution of K throught∗ without destruction.
Proof sketch. States outside Ω(M ) violate the meta-thresholds ΘM , contradicting Axiom 0.6. Any
operatorE mapping to such a state breaks AxiomΦ:2 and the compatibility conditions of Theorem 4. The
only way to keep the axioms consistent is that Ω(K) becomes empty (death) before reachings∗. Thus no
non-destructive evolution beyondt∗ exists.
P.8.4 Theorem on Birth of a New Dimension via Ψ
Theorem 6 (Birth of a new dimension). LetK M be a living continuum with structural tensionT (t)
monotonically increasing. If there exists a time t∗ such that T (t∗) > Θdim and there is an axis anew 2
A(M ) nA(K), then there exists and is unique (up to axis equivalence) a continuumK′ = Ψ(K;M ) with
dimK′ = dimK + 1.
Proof sketch. By Axiom Θ:4, crossing Θdim requires dimensional growth. By Axiom Ψ:1, any new
axis must come from A(M ) nA(K). By Axiom 0.9, local structural complexity is finite, so the set of
candidate axes is finite. Identifying axes that are equivalent with respect to their effect on Ω and Θ yields
a unique equivalence class of admissible new axes. Thus K′ is unique up to this equivalence and satisfies
dimK′ = dimK + 1.
470
P.8.5 Theorem on Death of a Continuum
Theorem 7 (Equivalence of death conditions). For a continuumK, the following conditions are equiv-
alent:
1. Ω(t∗) = ∅;
2. k(t) ! 0 ast !t∗;
3. cycle ! 1 and there exist no new cycles with finite frequency;
4. at least one threshold in Θdeath is violated.
Proof sketch. (1))(2): by Axiom K.2, a living continuum requires Ω 6= ∅; if Ω = ∅, then k = 0 .
(2))(3): by Axiom C.2 and k.1, non-zero continuumness requires at least one supporting cycle with finite
period;k ! 0 implies all such cycles degrade tocycle ! 1. (3) )(4): absence of supporting cycles and
diverging periods violate stability thresholds, which are part of Θdeath. (4) )(1): by Axiom D.3, violation
of any death threshold forces Ω = ∅. Thus all four conditions are equivalent characterizations of death.
P.8.6 Theorem on Phase Transition
Theorem 8 (Phase transition upon crossingΘcrit). LetK be a living continuum with structural tension
T (t). If there exists a time t∗ such that
Θcrit<T (t∗)< minfΘdim; Θdeathg;
then:
1. the admissible region Ω(t) undergoes a qualitative restructuring (splitting into new components or
merging of old ones);

Proof sketch. By definition of the critical threshold Θcrit (Axiom Θ:3), crossing it induces a structural
reorganization of Ω without forcing death or dimensional growth. The inequalities T < Θdim; Θdeath
guarantee that neither dimensional expansion nor death is triggered. Therefore the system undergoes a
phase transition within fixed dimension and non-zero continuumness.
P.8.7 Theorem on Impossibility of Degradational Evolution
Theorem 9 (No “backward” dimensional reduction for a living continuum). If there exists a time
t∗ such that
dimK(t∗ +dt)< dimK(t∗);
then the continuum K is dead at time t∗ +dt.

of dimension implies that the admissible region collapses to Ω = ∅ andk = 0. Thus, if the dimension is
strictly smaller att∗ +dt, the resulting configuration must be dead, and the change cannot be interpreted
as a genuine evolution of a living continuum.

P.9.3 Relation of S(K) tok(t),T (t), and (K)
Relation to continuumness k(t). Continuumnessk(t) reflects the quality of coherence and stability,

support rich dynamics;
• excessively highS(K) at fixed resources can reduce k(t) due to overload of thresholds Θ and insuﬀi-

Relation to structural tension T (t). Structural tensionT (t) tends to grow when:
• (Ω) increases without a corresponding increase in the number of axes A;
• Neff(Θ) increases at fixed axesA;
• flowsJ and cyclesC become misaligned or incoherent.
ThusT (t) can be expressed as a functional of the components SΩ;S A;S C;S Θ;S J . The phase thresholds
Θcrit, Θdim, and Θdeath appear as critical values for specific combinations of these components.
Relation to the temporal structure  (K). The temporal structure  (K) captures how quickly the
continuum can process its complexity:
• for fixedS(K), decreasingresponse andregen increases the probability of maintaining k(t)> 0;
• ifS(K) grows faster than the continuum can adapt its temporal constants, the system approaches a
collapse threshold Θcollapse.

P.9.4 Interpretation of the Complexity Metric
Interpretation of SΩ. SΩ captures the volume of admissible states. An increase in (Ω) without an
accompanying growth in axes raises structural tension.
Interpretation of SA. SA captures the dimensionality and the number of independent directions of
difference. Growth of dimK via Ψ allows tension to be redistributed but increases the cost of maintaining
structure.
Interpretation ofSC. SC measures the number and speed of cycles that support the life of the contin-
uum. Too few cycles make the system fragile; too many cycles at fixed resources can lead to competition
for flows and a drop in k(t).
Interpretation ofSΘ. SΘ captures the complexity of the threshold landscape. A large number of inde-
pendent thresholds makes Ω narrow and increases the risk of crossing death thresholds Θdeath.
Interpretation of SJ . SJ measures the intensity of motion inside the continuum. Insuﬀicient flows
make cycles impossible; excessive flows can erode the boundary @Ω and violate thresholds Θ.
Taken together, the components SΩ;S A;S C;S Θ;S J provide a quantitative measure of complexity
S(K) that supports the formal description of growth, phase transitions, and death of continua within
Core 1.2.

Q.1 Structural Experiments
The experimental programme of the Ontology of Continua (OC) provides the empirical and computational
foundation for testing structural predictions across all continuum levelsK0–K12. Unlike domain–specific
experiments contained in the per–level files (experiments_kX.tex), the present master module out-
lines the general methodology, validation strategies, and cross–domain principles that govern the design
and interpretation of experiments within OC.
Experiments in OC serve several structural functions:
• verifying the existence and saturation of thresholds Θ;
• tracking the behaviour of flowsJ under controlled perturbations;
• measuring cycle stabilityCstab and collapse dynamics;
• identifying birth conditions for new continua via Ψx→x+1;
• testing cross–level invariants that hold across physics, chemistry, biology, cognition, social systems,
and meta–theoretical continua.
Experimental design spans physical, chemical, biological, cognitive, institutional, and computational
modalities. Across those domains, every experiment still receives one structural interpretation in terms
of (Ω;A;P;J; Θ;@ Ω;C;k ).
Q.1.1 Purpose of Structural Experiments
Structural experiments aim to test not domain–specific phenomenology, but the general principles of
continuum dynamics. Every experiment targets at least one of the following claims:
1. Thresholds govern qualitative change. Phase transitions, regime shifts, collapse events, and di-
mensional births occur when structural tension T saturates a threshold Θcrit or Θdim.
2. Cycles maintain persistence. Stable cycles C underpin viability; their destruction predicts or
marks collapse.
3. Flows drive evolution. The balance between supporting and destructive flows determines system
stability.
4. Birth of new continua requires tension. Dimensional transitions arise only when T >Θdim.
5. Collapse is threshold–driven and irreversible. Violating Θdeath eliminates the admissible region
Ω, forcingk ! 0.
6. Cross–domain invariance. The same structural phenomena appear in K 2–K4 experiments (physi-
cal and chemical), in K4–K5 experiments (biological excitability), inK7–K8 (social collapse), and
inK9–K10 (paradigm coherence and theoretical collapse).
Q.1.2 T ypes of Experiments
OC distinguishes three major categories of experiments:
1. Physical / Chemical Experiments. These include tests of percolation thresholds, BKT transitions,
catalytic closure in RAF networks, vesicle stability under osmotic stress, curvature thresholds, and the
emergence of proto–excitability.
2. Biological / Cognitive Experiments. Tests include ion channel gating statistics, proto–spike genera-
tion, membrane recovery cycles, binding limits in cognitive tasks, and prediction thresholds in represen-
tational systems.
474
3. Social / Institutional / Theoretical Experiments. These evaluate trust thresholds, institutional sta-
bility, infrastructure cycles, and logical or model–theoretic coherence thresholds in K 9–K10.
Q.1.3 Universal Experiment Structure
Every experiment is represented by the tuple:
E = (initial state; perturbation; measurement;
threshold observation; cycle tracking; collapse / recovery criteria ):
This generic structure applies across all levels, where:
• perturbations drive flowsJ;
• measurements track potentials P and axesA;
• threshold observations determine whether Θ is approached or crossed;
• cycle tracking identifies the stability of C over time;
• collapse/recovery criteria map the behaviour of k(t).
Q.1.4 Measurement Protocols
OC introduces universal measurement protocols applicable to any continuum:
1. Threshold Tracking. MeasureP ,J, or A as a function of controlled perturbation to locate Θcrit,
Θstab, Θdim, or Θdeath.
2. Cycle Stability Analysis. Observe long–range coherence of C, compute:
S(C) = mind(Ω;@ Ω); C eff =

4. Birth Condition Evaluation. Detect the emergence of new axes when:

5. Cross–Domain Comparisons. Validate invariants across continuum levels.
Q.1.5 Computational Experiments
Many structural predictions of OC are most readily tested via computational experiments, including:
• percolation simulations forK2;
• stochastic RAF network generation forK3;
• membrane patch models and ion channel dynamics for K4–K5;
• predictive coding / binding models for K6;
• agent–based models of trust collapse for K7;
• infrastructure–energy co–evolution forK8;
• model–theoretic consistency checkers forK9–K10.
Computational experiments allow testing structural conditions that are diﬀicult or impossible to mea-
sure directly in natural systems.

Q.1.6 Experimental Validation Pipeline
The OC validation pipeline contains four universal stages:
1. Design: identify the structural prediction and the relevant K–level.
2. Perturbation: apply controlled changes to P ,A, orJ.
3. Measurement: measureT , Θ,C, andk(t).
4. Interpretation: evaluate structural behaviour relative to expected threshold saturation or cycle
dynamics.
Q.1.7 Relation to Falsifiability
All experiments in OC support falsifiability by targeting:
• prediction violations;
• threshold misalignment;
• cycle mismatch;
• incorrect dimensional birth conditions;
• unexpected collapse behaviour.
The master falsifiability module (Section 15) provides the system–level criteria, while the present
module organizes the experimental methodology.
Q.1.8 Cross-Level Generality
The experimental framework is intentionally cross–domain and cross–level. This universality is a defining
feature of OC and a central criterion for falsifiable theory construction: a structural prediction validated in
physics (K2) must have a corresponding instantiation in chemistry (K 3–K4), biology (K 4–K5), cognition
(K6), social systems ( K7–K8), and theoretical continua ( K9–K10), unless an explicit domain–specific
break is justified by the operator structure.

Q.1.10 Experiments for K0
The continuum level K0 represents the meta–ontological substrate of the Ontology of Continua. It does
not possess geometry, time, energy, flows, thresholds, or dynamics. Consequently, no physical or em-
pirical experiments can be performed on K0 in the usual sense. Instead, the validation of K0 proceeds
through structural and logical experiments: tests of consistency, definability, and well–posedness of the
transition operator Ψ0→1.
K0–experiments therefore evaluate theconditions of possibility for any continuum to exist, rather than
the behaviour of a continuum itself.
Q.1.11 Nature of K0 Experiments
BecauseK0 lacks:
• a state space Ω(K0),
• axesA,
• potentialsP ,
• flowsJ,
• thresholds Θ,
• cyclesC,
• and measurable time t,
experiments reduce to formal tests of the logical structure underlying continuum formation.
These tests target the following principles:
1. Non–contradiction of the ontological substrate. The foundational axioms governing K0 must
not generate paradoxes.
2. Minimal definability of a proto–parameter. A single real–valued proto–parameter p1 :S ! R
must be definable as a precondition for K1 (AxiomAp).
3. Connectedness of the proto–domain. The closure ofp1(S) must define a single connected interval
(a;b ) (AxiomAconn), ensuring that the resulting K1 continuum is one–dimensional and connected.
4. Absence of illicit structure. No geometry, metric, energy, or temporal order may be smuggled
intoK0. Any such appearance signals a violation of the axioms.
5. Well–posedness of Ψ0→1. The transition operator must produce a valid continuum K1 with:
Ω(K1); A1; P1; J1; Θ1; C1; k1(t)
in full agreement with the formal definition established in Core 1.3.
477
Q.1.12 T ype I Logical Experiments: Axiom Consistency Checks
These experiments verify that the axioms governing K0 form a coherent and non–contradictory set. The
tests include:
• consistency proofs for the absence of geometry;
• confirmation that no structure of dimension  1 is forced atK0;
• syntactic and semantic validation of the proto–parameter axioms;
• ensuring that no implicit metric or temporal order emerges from the axiom set.
Although not empirical, these experiments are essential: if K0 were inconsistent, the entire vertical
chainK1–K12 would collapse.
Q.1.13 T ype II Domain of Definition Experiments
These experiments validate the minimal domain S from which the proto–parameter p1 is defined. The
goal is to ensure that:
1. S contains no structure exceeding the axioms;
2. p1(S) is definable without prior geometry;
3. the mappingp1 does not introduce forbidden structure.
A successful experiment demonstrates that the raw substrate does not pre–encode any continuum and
is compatible with the birth of K1.
Q.1.14 T ype III Transition Experiments for Ψ0→1
The most important K0 experiments evaluate the correctness of the transition operator Ψ0→1.
These experiments ask:
• Does Ψ0→1 produce a state space Ω(K1) that is well–defined as a smooth 1D manifold?
• Does it produce the correct initial axis A1(x) = x?
• Does the resulting continuum satisfy all K1 axioms, including the definition of flows J1, energy E1,
tensionT1, and the trivial cycle Ctriv?
• Does the mapping avoid creating multiple connected components?
• Are the boundary conditions encoded by @Ω(K1) consistent with the source axioms at K0?
A failure of any of these tests indicates a structural error in the foundation of the entire model.
Q.1.15 T ype IV Meta–Consistency Experiments
Finally,K0 supports meta–theoretical consistency tests that ensure the entire vertical chain K0 !K1 !
K2 !    ! K12 can be defined without contradiction.
These experiments include:
• verifying thatK0 places no constraints incompatible with higher continua (e.g., physics or biology);
• checking that the transition maps Ψx→x+1 all have a well–defined domain containingK0 as substrate;
• confirming that no cyclic contradictions are introduced at the highest meta–levels ( K10–K12).
BecauseK0 is outside time, these experiments are purely structural and serve as the logical foundation
for the falsifiability pipeline.

Q.1.16 Summary
Experiments onK0 are not empirical but foundational. They verify:
• logical coherence of the axioms,
• definability of the proto–parameter,
• absence of illicit structure,
• well–posedness of Ψ0→1,
• compatibility with the entire K–hierarchy.
All higher experiments depend on the correctness of these structural tests.

Q.1.18 Objectives of K1 Experiments
Experiments at the level of K1 aim to verify:

Q.2 Falsifiability
Falsifiability in the Ontology of Continua (OC) differs fundamentally from standard empirical or phe-
nomenological falsifiability. Because OC is a structural theory, falsification proceeds through violations
of structural constraints rather than mismatches between numerical predictions and measurements. A
continuum exists only if it satisfies the axioms governing:
(Ω;A;P;J; Θ;@ Ω;C;k ):
Thus, any inconsistency between these components—or any failure of their dynamic evolution—is suﬀi-
cient to falsify a given instantiation of the theory.
This master file summarises the universal falsifiability programme for all continua K0–K12 and con-
nects it to the general operators F;G;H;Q;R;S;U , the threshold landscape, and the embedding-space
constraints ofMx.
521
Q.2.1 Structural Meaning of Falsifiability
A continuum Kx is falsified when the structure assigned to it cannot satisfy the OC axioms or when
its dynamic evolution contradicts the universal operators. The following structural criteria serve as the
foundation for falsifiability across all levels:
1. Violation of existence thresholds ( Θexist): If no configuration of (Ω;A;P;J ) can be made com-
patible with Θexist, the continuum cannot exist.
2. Boundary inconsistency: If@Ω cannot be defined such that it separates admissible from inadmis-
sible states, structural incoherence arises.
3. Operator incompatibility: IfF;G;H;Q;R;S;U cannot be consistently defined for the proposed
continuum, it is structurally impossible.
4. Cycle impossibility: If no non-trivial cycles C can be maintained, the continuum has k = 0 and
collapses.
5. Embedding-space violations: If Ω(Kx) 6 Ω(Mx), the continuum is falsified by Theorem 0.0
(embedding constraint).
6. Threshold contradictions: If Θcrit or Θdim cannot be satisfied, structural transitions become im-
possible.
7. Failure of monotonic dimension theorem: If dimKx decreases without collapse, OC is falsified.
These structural criteria are directly tied to the core OC axioms and therefore constitute universal
falsifiability conditions.
Q.2.2 Universal Falsifiability Criteria
Across all continua, the following universal conditions provide a complete falsification toolkit:
(F1) Incoherent State Space Ω. If Ω cannot form a connected, non-empty, admissible region under the
given axes and potentials, the continuum is impossible.
(F2) Impossible Axes A. If an axis cannot support at least two incompatible states (Theorem 3: mini-
mality of axes), the continuum collapses.
(F3) Potentials leaving admissible ranges (Pi /2 Dom(P )). Violations of potential bounds forceT !
1 or collapse.
(F4) Threshold incompatibility. If thresholds cannot be simultaneously satisfied:
Θexist< Θstab< Θcrit;
the continuum cannot stabilise.
(F5) Flow impossibility. If no supporting flowsJsupport exist,k(t) cannot remain positive.
(F6) Boundary collapse. If@Ω cannot remain well-defined underR, collapse is inevitable.
522
(F7) Operator inconsistency. If the evolution operator
K(t + ∆t) = E(K(t))
cannot be defined, the continuum is ruled out.
(F8) Violation of embedding constraints. If the embedding space Mx cannot host the continuum,
falsification is immediate.
Q.2.3 Cross-Level Falsifiability Structure
Falsifiability strengthens at higherK-levels because each continuum inherits constraints from all preced-
ing levels. Thus:
• K2 must satisfy all constraints of K0 andK1.
• K5 must satisfy all constraints of K0–K4.
• K10 must satisfy all constraints of K0–K9.
This inheritance principle ensures:
1. structural upward compatibility,
2. impossibility of “shortcut continua” skipping levels,
3. monotonic tightening of thresholds at each level,
4. cumulative constraints on dynamics and stability.
Cross-level falsifiability also allows identifying the level at which a model fails to satisfy OC, making
structural diagnosis possible.
Q.2.4 Falsifiability via Dynamics and Collapse
The dynamics of collapse provide additional, stringent falsification criteria.
(F9) Diverging structural tensionT . IfT (t) grows without bound and no axis, boundary, or potential
reconfiguration reduces it, collapse is guaranteed.

Q.2.8 Falsifiability of K0
The continuumK0 represents the minimal structural substrate of the Ontology of Continua. It is defined

not only K0 but also all higher continua, because the full hierarchy K1–K12 is built upon the existence
of a well-definedK0.
Q.2.9 Fundamental Falsifiability Principles for K0
The falsification ofK0 occurs when the structural triple (S; ∆; C) fails to satisfy the defining axioms:
• Axioms D1–D4: governing the set S of primitive distinctions and the minimal structural properties
of ∆.
• Axioms C1–C4′: governing the construction and compatibility of the composition operator C.
• Axiom 0.1 (Existence): which provides the minimal condition for a continuum to exist.
• Minimal threshold: Θ0 ="> 0, ensuring non-degeneracy.
Thus,K0 is falsified whenever the primitive combinatorial structure fails to meet these requirements.
Q.2.10 Structural Falsifiability Conditions
Several structural incompatibilities can invalidate K0:
(F0.1) Undefined or incoherentS. If the primitive set S of distinctions is empty or logically inconsis-

D1–D4 (irreflexivity, minimal consistency, closure under composition), then K0 is impossible.
(F0.3) Inconsistent composition C. If C cannot produce valid composite distinctions or violates C1–
C4′, structural coherence is lost.

Θ0 ="> 0

cycle violates the minimal continuity condition.
(F0.6) Contradiction in structural pairs. If the structural pair (S; ∆) cannot exist without contradic-
tion (violating the “structural pair axiom”), K0 is falsified.
Q.2.11 Boundary and Region Falsifiability

Q.2.12 Collapse and Non-Existence at K0

Q.2.119 Falsifiability of K12
The continuumK12 represents the highest definable level in the current Ontology of Continua: the space
of universal structural laws governing all possible meta-theoretical systems , including their birth, inter-
action, collapse, and representability. While K11 governs hyper-theories and meta-meta structures, K12
captures the conditions under which any structurally admissible universe of continua can exist . As such,
falsifiability of K12 is expressed through absolute constraints: violations result not in collapse to K11,
but in the impossibility of coherent structural organisation altogether.
Because of its universal role, falsifiability of K12 is determined by:
• global structural laws and their consistency,
• admissibility of all lower-level continuaK0 !K11,
• coherence of universal operators,
• existence and definability of Ω(K12),
• universal thresholds Θ12 limiting all structure.
If any criterion is violated, K12 cannot exist even momentarily.

(F12.2) Inconsistency across levels. If any lower level Kx (for 0  x  11) is incompatible with
universal structural laws,K12 becomes undefined.
(F12.3) Incompleteness of universal rules. If the universal rule set fails to determine behaviour of
continua in general,K12 cannot exist as a formal system.
(F12.4) Collapse of universal representability. If some continua cannot be represented in the universal
structural language, representability fails.
(F12.5) Violation of monotonicity of dimension. If dimension can decrease without collapse, or be-
have inconsistently with the general axioms, K12 is falsified.

R Unified Synthesis Support Dossiers
The main unified-synthesis section remains the canonical synthesis unit in the numbered Core 1.3 se-
quence of the manuscript. The material gathered here is retained as level-wise evidence support: it keeps
compact K-anchored theorem-support, empirical, falsifier, and packet dossiers available inside the flag-
ship volume while omitting the synthesis-section introduction and release-gate prose. Section 24 uses
the generated synthesis surface for the main K-level exposition. This appendix is the support-dossier
wrapper: it gives readers a single inspection location for the level-wise support files without turning them
into a second synthesis chapter. The main chapter states the synthesis, while this appendix carries the
dossier-oriented inspection copy. Compatibility support files are not input directly by the English plat-
inum master. A build variant must therefore choose either the compatibility synthesis-support master or
this appendix wrapper, never both. The full DFS compatibility stream still records those compatibility
entries for auditability, but the platinum master does not input the compatibility synthesis-support master.
The constants-and-parameters apparatus is part of the Appendix C data apparatus and is addressable there
as Appendix C.4; this support appendix does not create a second synthesis or a second top-level constants
appendix. Source stamp: releases/oc_core_1_3/editorial/OC_CORE_1_3_UNIFIED_SYNTH
ESIS_latest.json; current repository SHA and UTC generation timestamp are recorded inside that
JSON surface so this appendix does not freeze stale build metadata.
R.1 Level K0: structural conditions for any universe
Current closure status: PASS. Promotion blockers: none.
